docs.title: Complying with licenses
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: The recommendations in this page **are not legal advice.** They are provided  in good faith to help users navigate license attribution requirements.

docs.title: What are licenses?
docs.heading_path: Complying with licenses > What are licenses?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot is created and distributed under the MIT License <https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>_. It doesn't have a sole owner, as every contributor that submits code to the project does it under this same license and keeps ownership of their contribution.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: In the case of the MIT license, the only requirement is to include the license text somewhere in your game or derivative project.

docs.title: Inclusion
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: The license text must be made available to the user. The license doesn't specify how the text has to be included, but here are the most common approaches (you only need to implement one of them, not all).

docs.title: Credits screen
docs.heading_path: Complying with licenses > Inclusion > Credits screen
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Include the above license text somewhere in the credits screen. It can be at the bottom after showing the rest of the credits. Most large studios use this approach with open source licenses.

docs.title: Licenses screen
docs.heading_path: Complying with licenses > Inclusion > Licenses screen
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Some games have a special menu (often in the settings) to display licenses. This menu is typically accessed with a button called **Third-party Licenses** or **Open Source Licenses**.

docs.title: Output log
docs.heading_path: Complying with licenses > Inclusion > Output log
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Printing the license text using the :ref:print() <class_@GlobalScope_method_print> function may be enough on platforms where a global output log is readable. This is the case on desktop platforms, Android and HTML5 (but not iOS).

docs.title: Accompanying file
docs.heading_path: Complying with licenses > Inclusion > Accompanying file
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: If the game is distributed on desktop platforms, a file containing the license text can be added to the software that is installed to the user PC.

docs.title: Link to the license
docs.heading_path: Complying with licenses > Inclusion > Link to the license
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: The Godot Engine developers consider that a link to godotengine.org/license in your game documentation or credits would be an acceptable way to satisfy the license terms.

docs.title: Third-party licenses
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot itself contains software written by third parties <https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/thirdparty/README.md>_, which is compatible with, but not covered by Godot's MIT license.

docs.title: What can I do with Godot? How much does it cost? What are the license terms?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > What can I do with Godot? How much does it cost? What are the license terms?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot is Free and open source Software <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_and_open_source_software>_ available under the OSI-approved <https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>_ MIT license. This means it is free as in "free speech" as well as in "free beer."

docs.title: Which platforms are supported by Godot?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Which platforms are supported by Godot?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs

docs.title: Which programming languages are supported in Godot?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Which programming languages are supported in Godot?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: The officially supported languages for Godot are GDScript, C#, and C++. See the subcategories for each language in the :ref:scripting <toc-learn-scripting> section.

docs.title: What is GDScript and why should I use it?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > What is GDScript and why should I use it?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: GDScript is Godot's integrated scripting language. It was built from the ground up to maximize Godot's potential in the least amount of code, affording both novice and expert developers alike to capitalize on Godot's strengths as fast as possible. If you've ever written anything…

docs.title: What were the motivations behind creating GDScript?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > What were the motivations behind creating GDScript?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: In the early days, the engine used the Lua <https://www.lua.org>__ scripting language. Lua can be fast thanks to LuaJIT, but creating bindings to an object-oriented system (by using fallbacks) was complex and slow and took an enormous amount of code. After some experiments with…

docs.title: Which programming language is fastest?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Which programming language is fastest?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: In most games, the *scripting language* itself is not the cause of performance problems. Instead, performance is slowed by inefficient algorithms (which are slow in all languages), by GPU performance, or by the common C++ engine code like physics or navigation. All languages…

docs.title: What 3D model formats does Godot support?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > What 3D model formats does Godot support?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: You can find detailed information on supported formats, how to export them from your 3D modeling software, and how to import them for Godot in the :ref:doc_importing_3d_scenes documentation.

docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: The aim of Godot is to create a free and open source MIT-licensed engine that is modular and extendable. There are no plans for the core engine development community to support any third-party, closed-source/proprietary SDKs, as integrating with these would go against Godot's…

docs.snippet: For extending Godot, like creating Godot Editor plugins or adding support for additional languages, take a look at :ref:EditorPlugins <doc_making_plugins> and tool scripts.

docs.snippet: Drag the extracted Godot application to /Applications/Godot.app, then drag it to the Dock if desired. Spotlight will be able to find Godot as long as it's in /Applications or ~/Applications.

docs.title: Is the Godot editor a portable application?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Is the Godot editor a portable application?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: In its default configuration, Godot is *semi-portable*. Its executable can run from any location (including non-writable locations) and never requires administrator privileges.

docs.title: Why does Godot aim to keep its core feature set small?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Why does Godot aim to keep its core feature set small?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot intentionally does not include features that can be implemented by add-ons unless they are used very often. One example of something not used often is advanced artificial intelligence functionality.

docs.snippet: This question pops up often and it's probably thanks to the misunderstanding created by Apple when they originally doubled the resolution of their devices. It made people think that having the same assets in different resolutions was a good idea, so many continued towards that…

docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > When is the next release of Godot out?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: When it's ready! See :ref:doc_release_policy_when_is_next_release_out for more information.

docs.title: Which Godot version should I use for a new project?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Which Godot version should I use for a new project?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: We recommend using Godot 4.x for new projects, but depending on the feature set you need, it may be better to use 3.x instead. See :ref:doc_release_policy_which_version_should_i_use for more information.

docs.title: Should I upgrade my project to use new Godot versions?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Should I upgrade my project to use new Godot versions?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Some new versions are safer to upgrade to than others. In general, whether you should upgrade depends on your project's circumstances. See :ref:doc_release_policy_should_i_upgrade_my_project for more information.

docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Awesome! As an open source project, Godot thrives off of the innovation and the ambition of developers like you.

docs.title: I have a great idea for Godot. How can I share it?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > I have a great idea for Godot. How can I share it?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: We are always looking for suggestions about how to improve the engine. User feedback is the main driving force behind our decision-making process, and limitations that you might face while working on your project are a great data point for us when considering engine enhancements.

docs.title: Is it possible to use Godot to create non-game applications?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Is it possible to use Godot to create non-game applications?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Yes! Godot features an extensive built-in UI system, and its small distribution size can make it a suitable alternative to frameworks like Electron or Qt.

docs.title: Is it possible to use Godot as a library?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Is it possible to use Godot as a library?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: If you are looking to make a game with Godot, keep in mind Godot is designed to be used with its editor. We recommend you give it a try, as it will most likely save you time in the long term.

docs.title: What user interface toolkit does Godot use?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > What user interface toolkit does Godot use?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot does not use a standard :abbr:GUI (Graphical User Interface) toolkit like GTK, Qt or wxWidgets. Instead, Godot uses its own user interface toolkit, which is always rendered using hardware acceleration. There is no built-in software fallback, although external solutions…

docs.title: Why does Godot use the SCons build system?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Why does Godot use the SCons build system?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot uses the SCons <https://www.scons.org/>__ build system. There are no plans to switch to a different build system in the near future. There are many reasons why we have chosen SCons over other alternatives. For example:

docs.title: Why does Godot not use STL (Standard Template Library)?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Why does Godot not use STL (Standard Template Library)?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Like many other libraries (Qt as an example), Godot does not make use of STL (with a few exceptions such as threading primitives). We believe STL is a great general-purpose library, but we had special requirements for Godot.

docs.title: Why does Godot not use exceptions?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Why does Godot not use exceptions?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: We believe games should not crash, no matter what. If an unexpected situation happens, Godot will print an error (which can be traced even to script), but then it will try to recover as gracefully as possible and keep going.

docs.title: Does Godot use an ECS (Entity Component System)?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Does Godot use an ECS (Entity Component System)?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Godot does **not** use an ECS and relies on inheritance instead. While there is no universally better approach, we found that using an inheritance-based approach resulted in better usability while still being fast enough for most use cases.

docs.title: Why does Godot not force users to implement DOD (Data-Oriented Design)?
docs.heading_path: Frequently asked questions > Why does Godot not force users to implement DOD (Data-Oriented Design)?
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: While Godot internally attempts to use cache coherency as much as possible, we believe users don't need to be forced to use DOD practices.

docs.snippet: This page is a high-level overview of Godot 4's internal renderer design. It does not apply to previous Godot versions.

docs.title: Forward+

docs.snippet: Clustered lighting uses a compute shader to group lights into a 3D frustum aligned grid. Then, at render time, pixels can lookup what lights affect the grid cell they are in and only run light calculations for lights that might affect that pixel.

docs.snippet: In this part, we'll add the ability to jump and squash the monsters. In the next lesson, we'll make the player die when a monster hits them on the ground.

docs.title: Controlling physics interactions

docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: Physics bodies have access to two complementary properties: layers and masks. Layers define on which physics layer(s) an object is.

docs.heading_path: Jumping and squashing monsters > Controlling physics interactions > Setting layer names
docs.attribution: © Godot Engine contributors — MIT, via godotengine/godot-docs
docs.snippet: In the left menu, navigate down to *Layer Names -> 3D Physics*. You can see a list of layers with a field next to each of them on the right. You can set their names there. Name the first three layers *player*, *enemies*, and *world*, respectively.
